Answer this question from a curated study note: How is a synapse like a bacterium?

A synapse, about the same size as a bacterium, contains a plethora of proteins that are continually degraded and renewed. Through an unending cycle of molecular death and rebirth, synapses morph their composition and structure to recent events. Fluctuations in membrane voltage, release and uptake of neurotransmitters and ions, frequency and shape of action potentials are all relevant. These transient effects can regulate local processes such as protein modification, assembly of protein complexes, and intracellular movements. Local physiology can even influence events in the distant cell nucleus such as gene expression and alternative RNA splicing. By embedding a record of its past in its molecular structure, each synapse becomes distinct, unique. Its response to patterns of activity will be distinct from that of any other synapse. Most of this variation will be meaningless, just chemical noise. But a significant fraction of the multiple forms will be significant and will mean something in terms of the outside world.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Four modes of being in school in The Disengaged Teen:

• Resister. When kids resist, they struggle silently with profound feelings of inadequacy or invisibility, which they communicate by ignoring homework, playing sick, skipping class, or acting out.

• Passenger. When kids coast along, consistently doing the bare minimum and complaining that classes are pointless. They need help connecting school to their skills, interests, or learning needs.

• Achiever. When kids show up, do the work, and get consistently high grades, their self-worth can become tied to high performance. Their disengagement is invisible, fueling a fear of failure and putting them at risk for mental health challenges.

• Explorer. When kids are driven by internal curiosity rather than just external expectations, they investigate the questions they care about and persist to achieve their goals.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Agriculture vs. textiles in terms of automation:

To see why the elasticity of substitution matters, let’s consider an example from economic history: agriculture. In many pre-industrial societies, agriculture accounted for the majority of GDP. However, as agricultural processes became increasingly automated, the share of agriculture in the economy shrank dramatically. Today, in the United States, agricultural production represents only about 1-2% of GDP.

This example illustrates a critical point: as automation transforms a sector, the importance of that sector within the broader economy can decline. This is because as productivity increases and output grows, additional gains in efficiency tend to contribute less and less to GDP. As a consequence, automation in these cases will have a muted effect on overall economic growth.

However, this pattern is not universal. Consider the case of textiles during the Industrial Revolution in Great Britain. The introduction of powered looms and spinning machines made textile production far more efficient, and instead of shrinking in importance, the textile industry grew to become a key part of Britain’s economy. In this case, automation led to a significant expansion of the sector’s share in the economy, meaning that automating textiles had an outsized, large impact on overall economic growth.

Answer this question from a curated study note: How does Derek Silvers ask mentors for help?

‍"I have three mentors.

When I’m stuck on a problem and need their help, I take the time to write a good description of my dilemma, before reaching out to them. I summarize the context, the problem, my options, and my thoughts on each. I make it as succinct as possible so as not to waste their time.

Before sending it, I try to predict what they’ll say. Then I go back and update what I wrote to address these obvious points in advance.

Finally, I try again to predict what they’ll say to this, based on what they’ve said in the past and what I know of their philosophy. Then, after this whole process, I realize I don’t need to bother them because the answer is now clear… None of them know they are my mentors.”

- Derek Sivers

Answer this question from a curated study note: Maybe not language 200k years ago but 75k. why?

1. Traditional Model of Language Evolution: Older models suggested that human cognitive abilities, including language, evolved over 200,000 years ago as Homo sapiens emerged. The idea was that these abilities didn’t confer a competitive advantage until 70,000–50,000 years ago, when humans showed signs of “Behavioral Modernity” (like art and complex tools) and outcompeted other hominin species.

2. Critique of the Traditional Model: Genetic research over the past two decades, especially work by David Reich and others, challenges this timeline. Findings show that key genetic traits linked to cognition and IQ have continued evolving over the past 10,000 years. This implies that cognitive evolution was ongoing even after modern humans spread globally, contradicting the idea of a 200,000-year cognitive “off-switch.”

3. Cultural Feedback Loops: Some scientists, like Reich, propose that the growth in social and cultural complexity, rather than purely biological evolution, might have enabled language and symbolic thought. As human groups became larger and more interconnected, they developed collective knowledge, tools, and cultural practices, creating a feedback loop that reinforced symbolic abilities and possibly language itself.

4. Genetic Factors in Recent Evolution: The article also discusses how recent genetic studies show selective pressures on traits related to intelligence and social cognition, which continued shaping the human brain. This may have contributed to the development of language capabilities much later than originally thought—potentially within the last 50,000 years, aligning with the “Sapient Paradox” (why abstract thought emerged relatively late in human history).

5. Physical Adaptations for Language: Genetic changes in the human vocal tract (e.g., larynx, pharynx) unique to our lineage suggest that humans developed the physical capacity for complex language only within the last few hundred thousand years, perhaps even as recently as 50,000–100,000 years ago.

6. Symbolic Thought and Self-Consciousness: Some theories propose that symbolic thought, self-consciousness, and perhaps a sense of self emerged alongside language, facilitated by cultural and genetic co-evolution. This evolution might have been a gradual process that sparked significant cognitive advancements only when culture and knowledge reached critical mass.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Why do elements have more neutrons as they gain atomic mass? (Stability)

🔩 Why Heavier Elements Have More Neutrons:

As atomic number (Z = # of protons) increases, atoms need more neutrons to stay stable. Here’s why:

⚖️ 1. Protons repel each other

Protons are positively charged, so more of them = more electrostatic repulsion.

That makes the nucleus want to blow apart.

🧲 2. Neutrons help hold the nucleus together

Neutrons add strong nuclear force (which is attractive) without adding repulsion (they’re neutral).

So, they “glue” the protons together.

4000-3000: Writing. Forces of nature.
3000-2000: Personified divinities

The earliest evidence of Mesopotamian religion dates to the mid-4th millennium BC, coincides with the invention of writing, and involved the worship of forces of nature as providers of sustenance.

Answer this question from a curated study note: WBW:

I like to think of a human’s genome as a little handful of sand:

A human genome is about 3 billion letters long, or 3 billion grains of sand. Imagine four handfuls of sand representing the genomes of your four grandparents, each a different color sand: red, yellow, green, blue. Your dad, whose parents have red and yellow sand, each contributed 50% of his genome. So his DNA is half red, half yellow. Your mom’s DNA, likewise, is half green, half blue. Then, each of your parents contributed 50% of their DNA to make up 50% of your genome—but which 50% of their DNA ended up in you is variable. Your dad is half red, half yellow, but maybe the chunk of DNA he gave to you is 40% red, 60% yellow. That would mean you are a bit more related to your yellow grandparent than you are to your red grandparent. Meanwhile, your sister might have gotten the reverse proportions from your dad and be more related to the red grandparent. Your brother might have something closer to your proportion, which also means that you’re more genetically similar to your brother than you are to your sister.

Answer this question from a curated study note: What does shigella do to us?

Shigella is a bacterium that causes shigellosis, an infection that primarily affects the colon (large intestine). Its effects include:

1. Invasion of Colonic Epithelial Cells: Shigella invades the epithelial cells lining the colon, leading to cell death and ulceration.

2. Inflammation: The invasion triggers a strong immune response, causing inflammation and swelling of the colon.

3. Diarrhea: The infection results in frequent, small-volume stools that may be watery or contain mucus and blood.

4. Cytotoxin Production: Shigella produces Shiga toxin, which damages the intestinal lining and can lead to severe symptoms, including bloody diarrhea.

5. Systemic Symptoms: In severe cases, the toxin can enter the bloodstream, potentially causing systemic effects like hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), especially in children.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Secrecy during atomic bomb:

Szilard made fermi keep graphite secret

He conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, patented the idea in 1936, and in late 1939 wrote the letter for Albert Einstein's signature that resulted in the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb.

In the fall of 1940, Fermi had finished new carbon absorption measurements on graphite, suggesting graphite was a viable moderator for a bomb. Szilard assaulted Fermi with yet another secrecy appeal. “At this time Fermi really lost his temper; he really thought this was absurd,” Szilard recounted. Luckily, further appeals were eventually successful, and Fermi reluctantly refrained from publishing his graphite results.

At the same time, the German project had narrowed down on two possible moderator materials: graphite and heavy water. In early 1941 at Heidelberg, Walther Bothe made an incorrect measurement on the absorption cross-section of graphite, and concluded that graphite would absorb too many neutrons to sustain a chain reaction. Since Fermi had kept his result secret, the Germans did not have Fermi’s measurements to check against, and to correct the error. This was crucial: it led the German project to pursue heavy water instead—a decisive wrong path that ultimately doomed the German nuclear weapons effort.

In the early decades, critics said the schools were too academic and were failing to prepare students for an industrial economy. In the 1940s, critics complained that the schools were underfunded, overcrowded, and unprepared for the postwar economy and the atomic age.

In the early 1950s, critics assailed the schools for their lack of academic rigor. In response, Congress passed the National Defense Education Act of 1958.

In the 1960s, the nation “discovered” poverty, and the schools were again subject to searing criticism because they reflected the prejudices of the larger society. Congress reacted with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning racial discrimination in the schools and other public institutions.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the schools were lambasted by critics who discerned, as author Charles Silberman put it, a “crisis in the classroom” due to “mindlessness” and the routinization of education. In 1983, a federal commission declared that the United States was “a nation at risk” because of the failings of our schools. Since the late 1990s, the crisis in education has centered on the achievement gap between children of different races.

Answer this question from a curated study note: How to think about computers/embedded systems for every human?

1 computer/smartphone/server for every person (10B)

10 embedded systems (cars/household/erc 100 in the West, 1 in Africa)

Perhaps an average of 15 for every man, woman and child on this planet. Seems high? Read on.

In another answer ( How many computers are in each USA household? ) I estimated the number of embedded computers in an average household at “several dozen”.

Most of the embedded systems a household are sitting in your garage — a typical new car has 50–60 microcontrollers in it, with 10 million lines of code, and and a high-end Mercedes or BMW has over 100, with over 100 million lines of code — much more than a 787 Dreamliner. But the average household doesn’t have a BMW, or even a new car — in fact the average US automobile is now 11.5 years old.

I think an estimate of at least several dozen —perhaps 75 or so — for an average household is reasonable. This article, from way back in 2003, estimated 40.

If we take 75 times the number of households in the US (133 million), we get almost 10 billion. That’s just in the US. And that’s just households and doesn’t include all the commercial buildings and vehicles and other uses.

So just in the US, perhaps 15–20 billion systems. Worldwide, there are over 1500 households. But the rest of the world doesn’t have anywhere near as many cars per capita as the US — and since that’s where most of the embedded systems are, one can assume the US has the lead.

So worldwide, I am guessing 75 to 100 billion embedded systems currently in use.

As a cross-check, according to this article, 31 billion microcontrollers were shipped in 2016, and the number is expected to grow to 50 billion in 2019. Some embedded system include more than one microcontroller, so there is not a 1–1 correspondence. But even so my guess of 75–100 billion may be on the low side. It looks like the number will certainly be over the century mark by next year.

The number of embedded systems per household should rapidly increase, as people trade in their older vehicles for new ones with dozens of microcontrollers, replace their light bulbs with LED versions, each with its own microcontroller, and add Amazon Alexa and Google Home-enabled devices in their homes.

In comparison, there are something over two billions PCs in the world, a little over a billion tablet computers, and almost five billion smartphones.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Overview of Anil Seth’s preprint “Conscious Artificial Intelligence and Biological Naturalism”:

1. Computational Functionalism Is Not a Given

• Seth challenges the common assumption that consciousness depends only on the functional or computational organization of a system (i.e., that any suitably complex or correct algorithm running on any substrate could be conscious).

• He notes that standard digital or Turing-based computation might be insufficient for consciousness because biological brain processes are deeply “entangled” with their substrate – for example, continuous dynamics, energy usage, metabolic processes, and other non-computational factors.

2. Biological Naturalism

• Seth makes the case for what he calls “biological naturalism”: the view that consciousness is specifically a property of living systems (or systems that share critical characteristics of living organisms).

• This stance does not assume “magic” or vitalism but stresses that being alive—maintaining one’s own material integrity (autopoiesis), staying out of thermodynamic equilibrium, and constantly regulating the internal physiology—is central to why and how human consciousness exists.

Answer this question from a curated study note: What is the postal system of the cell?

It begins with the linguistic code of genes (RNA) that is translated to write the letter (the protein). The protein is written, or synthesized, by the cell’s letter writer (the ribosome), which then posts it to the mailbox (the pore by which the protein enters the ER). I recently wrote about my mindset towards giving, titled: We Should Tithe More! However, creating organic, bottom-up, “selfless/cooperative” behavior is difficult (without some centralized coordination mechanism for cooperation, e.g. the government). This article explores one way to organically catalyze cooperation. Applying Theory of Cooperation to Universal Tithing In Robert Axelrod’s classic book, The Evolution of Cooperation, he outlines his “Theory of Cooperation” as an explanation for why cooperation organically emerges

without a centralized institution. Through Prisoner’s Dilemma modeling and biological and social case studies, Axelrod determines 4 characteristics that correlate with success (in a 2-agent repeated game scenario). They are: Start with Cooperation (don’t start with defection) Retaliate Quickly (if they defect, you should defect) Forgive Quickly (after retaliation, forgive them by cooperating again) Be Consistent (clarity allows others to cooperate with you) We can apply this to Universal Tithing: Start with Cooperation: I start by assuming that I’ll be tithing to help others (and that they’ll tithe as well). (I don’t create “excuses” to not tithe like, “others don’t do it, so I don’t do it.”) Retaliate Quickly: This is difficult to map into the tithing system. What counts as defection? (Especially when we’re trying to say “tithe an amount of money to the charities you’d like. Do what feels right to you!”) Should a defection be “not tithing enough given a certain income”? Or “not thinking enough about Effective Altruist impact when you give”? Or maybe “continuing to hold a zero-sum/scarcity-driven mindset”? And then if they “defect” (by not giving or whatever), then how can one “retaliate”? I was never really giving them anything in the 1st place, so how could I “punish” them? Given those (very much still open) questions, my instinct is to have a rule similar to this: “if you make over $40,000 and don’t tithe at least 5% to charity, then I will be much less likely to work with you or help you”. It’s still a bit awkward. Thoughts? Forgive Quickly: Pretty simple given my proposed rule above. If someone starts to give, then I’d be happy to collaborate with / help them!

In it's purely technical/developer form, it's a proto-version of Lean/Agile and Facebook's "move fast and break things" model. i.e. Optimize for quick iteration cycles, optimizing for customer-facing UX, rather

than for top-down "functionality"/minimizing technical debt. (See Gwern's Bitcoin is Worse is Better.) Better is Worse Surprisingly, very little has been written about the reverse of Worse is Better (WiB), Better is Worse (BiW!). With Better is Worse, the initial "goodness" of the thing eventually leads to a "negative" outcome. Let's look at a specific example: The Innovator's Dilemma: A company is "better" by making money from its current customers, continuing to serve them, and moving up the cost curve. But because the company is "winning", it doesn't "see" some of the niche/lower cost products that startups are building. By the time the big company realizes this, it's too late and it's been "disrupted" by the startup. In other words, Better is (in the end) Worse. BiW and WiB as Multi-Perspective Thinking I find myself increasingly using BiW and WiB outside the technical context. In fact, I think it's a great way to push for multi-perspective thinking. i.e. For anything with a "good" outcome, search for the "bad" outcome as well (and vice versa). Some other examples: Erik Torenberg applies Better is Worse to jocks, here: Why do high school jocks tend to be less cool in their adult years? Innovator’s dilemma. Since they’re too busy serving existing customers, they can’t invest in R&D. What got them here (athleticism/looks -> popularity) often won’t get them there (expertise -> wealth, status). — Erik Torenberg (@eriktorenberg) May 8, 2019 I use Better is Worse to understand my "superpower/shadow" dynamics. i.e. My "superpowers" (things I'm good at) can lead to negative outcomes. But it can also manifest through leveraging the "superpower" for negative outcomes. (e.g. In childhood, I used to use my ability to understand others to "be a class clown/play games/manipulate" my peers.) In other words, Better is Worse because you don't cultivate a holistic self (because you could get by without

it) and because you can use your abilities for bad ends. The creative framework that Mark Rosewater loves, "Constraints Breed Creativity", is an example of Worse is Better. Initially, you may think the constraint it bad—it puts you in a box! But in fact the constraint allows you to be more creative. People often use Worse is Better for filtering to "get the right people". Early Adopters are generally an example of this. You don't want rando's using your initial product, so you release a crappy version of it (Worse) that leads to only the "true believer" Early Adopters to use it and give you feedback (Better). You can also use this for events: make an event at a super early time and don't serve food. It's "Worse", but only the super passionate people will come (Better). We did this for the 1st year of ETHDenver as well—make the hacker application super long so only passionate hackers apply (not random ICO folks). Related: I heard that MakerDAO made their documentation purposely confusing at first so that only sharp true believers could make it through (and be part of their early community). In some ways, you can think of BiW and WiB as abstract ways to talk about a balancing feedback loop. This is in contrast to a reinforcing feedback loop, like Liquidity Begets Liquidity, where Better is Better or Worse is Worse. In the end, my key points are: We should use Better is Worse in addition to Worse is Better We should more often apply them to domains outside of programming—they are useful for multi-perspective/systems thinking generally.
